subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that the equations of common tangents to the circle x² + y² = 2a² and the parabola y² = 8ax are y = ±(x + 2a).

mark_split.label: Write the tangent to the parabola with slope m
Apply the tangential condition to the circle
Solve for m² and reject the impossible root
Write the combined equation of both tangents

steps.label: Write the tangent with slope m
steps.margin_note: First two marks: matching the given parabola to the standard form and writing its tangent.
steps.why: Writing y² = 8ax as y² = 4(2a)x matches it to the standard form y² = 4Ax with A = 2a, so the standard tangent formula y = mx + A/m can be used directly with A replaced by 2a.
common_mistakes: Reading 4a from y² = 8ax instead of comparing to 4Ax and getting A = 2a.
Writing the tangent as y = mx + a/m, forgetting the extra factor of 2.
steps.memory_tip: y² = 8ax is y² = 4(2a)x — the number multiplying x is always 4 times the tangent's own a-value.

steps.label: Apply the circle's tangential condition
steps.margin_note: Two marks for setting up the shared condition — this is where the two curves meet in the algebra.
lines: A line y = mx + c touches the circle
x² + y² = r² when c² = r²(1 + m²).

lines.text: (the distance from (0, 0) to mx − y + c = 0 is
|c|/√(1 + m²), and it must equal r)
(a common tangent must touch both curves)

steps.why: The tangential condition c² = r²(1+m²) is the algebraic test for a line touching a circle centred at the origin — it is applied here with c taken from the parabola's own tangent line, which forces the same line to touch both curves at once.
common_mistakes: Using the tangential condition for the parabola on the circle equation, or vice versa.
Writing r² = 2a instead of 2a² (dropping the square).
steps.memory_tip: One line, two conditions: c = 2a/m makes it a tangent to the parabola, and c² = r²(1+m²) makes the same line a tangent to the circle.
lines_compact: A line y = mx + c touches the circle
x² + y² = r² when c² = r²(1 + m²).

steps.label: Solve for m² and reject the impossible root
steps.margin_note: Two marks for the algebra and the rejection of the impossible root — both are needed for full credit.

lines.text: This is a quadratic in m². Two numbers with

lines: m² = 1 or m² = −2; m² cannot be negative,
steps.why: The equation is a quadratic in the new variable m², so it factors the same way any quadratic does; the root m² = −2 is thrown out immediately because a real slope always squares to something zero or positive.
common_mistakes: Stopping at m⁴ + m² − 2 = 0 without factoring, or factoring it wrong.
Keeping both roots m² = 1 and m² = −2 instead of rejecting the impossible one.
steps.memory_tip: m⁴ + m² − 2 factors as (m² − 1)(m² + 2) — the second bracket can never be zero for a real m, so only m² = 1 survives.
lines_compact: m² = 1 or m² = −2; m² cannot be negative,

steps.label: Write the combined tangent equation
steps.margin_note: Last mark for combining both lines into the single boxed ± form the question asks for.
steps.why: Each value of m gives its own value of c through c = 2a/m, and writing the two resulting lines together as one ± equation is simply a compact way to state both at once.
common_mistakes: Pairing m = 1 with c = −2a or m = −1 with c = 2a — the sign of c always follows the sign of m through c = 2a/m.
Leaving the two lines unwritten together as two separate boxed answers instead of the single ± form asked for.
steps.memory_tip: c always equals 2a divided by m, so the sign of c copies the sign of m.

insider_note: Both values m² = 1 and m² = −2 are expected to be considered, even though only m² = 1 gives a real slope m, because the square of a real number is never negative — stating why m² = −2 is rejected is worth the mark that a jump straight to m² = 1 would lose.
